COURSES.name: Foundations of Leadership
COURSES.desc: Builds the everyday operating habits a first leadership role asks for: taking work end to end, handing it over cleanly, and saying the hard thing early. For people stepping up in the job they are already in.

COURSES.name: Leading High-Performing Teams
COURSES.desc: Develops the craft of holding a team steady through conflict, coaching rather than fixing, and running a weekly rhythm people leave knowing what to do. For those already leading who want the team to carry more.

COURSES.name: Executive Strategy & Vision
COURSES.desc: Turns a leader outward: setting direction under incomplete information, telling a decision you can reverse from one you cannot, and carrying a team through a change nobody chose. For people building toward ownership.

COURSES.name: Communicating with Impact
COURSES.desc: Sharpens how a message lands: opening a hard conversation without an ambush, giving feedback that changes what happens next, and reading what a room is not saying. Useful at every level and every intent.

COURSES.name: Influencing Without Authority
COURSES.desc: The skill of moving work through people who do not report to you: building trust at speed, managing up, and making small commitments in public and keeping them. For those leading across a business, not just down a line.

COURSES.name: Communication Essentials
COURSES.desc: The groundwork of being understood at work: saying what you mean in one sentence other people repeat, listening for what matters, and giving your manager the version of a problem they can act on. The entry course.

COURSES.name: Team Leadership
COURSES.desc: Everything a group needs from the person in front of it: delegation without drop-off, repair after a working relationship breaks, and holding the line while two people are still angry. For established team leads.

COURSES.name: Leading Through Change
COURSES.desc: How to keep the work going while the ground moves: saying what you know and what you do not, taking the heat out of a disagreement without avoiding it, and leading people through a change they did not choose. The senior Builder course.

PAST_IVS.tal:
Tal suggests Explorer – E3. On the transcript Maryam reads as someone who reasons from consequence, not policy: she starts from the people a decision lands on and works back.

What earns E3: three worked examples that each carry a date and a name, and a reorganization she can explain call by call rather than in outline.

What holds it below E4: the growth is coaching rather than fixing. She still solves a problem herself where developing someone else would be the E4 move.

Ask in the room: one time she coached a report through a hard call, and what changed. A real outcome there is what would put E4 on the table.
PAST_IVS.strengths: You reason from consequence to people, not policy. Three examples, each with a date and a name attached.
PAST_IVS.growth: Delegation, and coaching rather than fixing. Chapters 4 and 12 are built on exactly this.
PAST_IVS.note: She talks cautiously, but she has already run a reorganization and can explain every call she made in it. That is an E3, not an E2.
PAST_IVS.review: Dana was direct and fair. She pushed on the parts I was vague about and I left knowing exactly what to work on.

PAST_IVS.tal:
Tal suggests Explorer – E2, at the E2 to E3 boundary. Ava is clear about the outcomes she owns and honest about the ones she missed.

What earns the read: she separates the decision from the result, so a miss is examined rather than explained away.

What holds it at E2: almost every example is her acting alone. There is little evidence yet of coaching someone else through a hard call.

Ask in the room: one time she brought a second person into the work and developed them. That is the evidence that moves this to E3.
PAST_IVS.strengths: Clear on the outcomes you own and honest about the ones you missed. You separate the decision from the result when you talk it through.
PAST_IVS.growth: Bring a second person into the story. Most examples are you acting alone rather than you developing someone else.
PAST_IVS.note: Solid and self-aware. I would want to see one example of her coaching a report before I called it above E2.
PAST_IVS.review: A calm, well-structured hour. Fair questions and useful pointers on where to focus next.

PAST_IVS.tal:
Tal suggests Explorer – E4. Jordan reads as someone who can frame a trade-off across teams and name what each option costs.

What earns E4: he holds two competing priorities in view at once, and his examples span more than one team rather than one desk.

What keeps it at E4 rather than higher: he leaves the ending open. He explores a decision well but does not always close it.

Ask in the room: one decision he closed cleanly under pressure, and how it landed. A clean close is what confirms E4 and hints at more.
PAST_IVS.strengths: You hold two competing priorities in view and can say what each one costs. Examples span more than one team.
PAST_IVS.growth: Tighten how you close a decision. You explore well but the ending is sometimes left open.
PAST_IVS.note: Reads a room and a roadmap at the same time. Comfortable at E4.
PAST_IVS.review: Priya asked sharp questions and gave me a genuinely useful read on my blind spots.

PAST_IVS.tal:
Tal suggests Explorer – E2. Sophia reads as a dependable, clear operator: she keeps people informed without being asked and her handovers are clean.

What earns E2: reliable delivery and communication you do not have to chase, across a full cycle of work.

What holds it below E3: she tends to absorb a problem before naming it. She handles issues well once they land, but raises them late.

Ask in the room: one problem she named early, before it became urgent. The growth here is timing, not capability, and that is what moves it to E3.
PAST_IVS.strengths: Dependable and clear. You keep people informed without being asked and your handovers are clean.
PAST_IVS.growth: Name a problem earlier. You handle issues well once they land but you tend to absorb them first.
PAST_IVS.note: Trustworthy operator. The growth is timing, not capability.
PAST_IVS.review: Marcus put me at ease and the feedback was specific and kind.

Leading a project where two of my team disagreed on scope. I made the call in the end, but I am not sure I brought them along with me.

Covering for my manager for six weeks. I kept things running but struggled to hand off the parts I usually hold myself.
Giving difficult feedback to a peer. It landed fine in the end, but I sat on it far too long first.
Rolling out a process the team pushed back on. I want to talk about how I read the room and where I lost people.

sessions.title: Sessions
sessions.desc: How long an internal user’s session may sit idle before it ends. A change applies to sessions started after it; one already running keeps the period it started under.

fields.hint: Internal accounts only. Candidates and agents have no inactivity sign-out.

exports.title: Exports
exports.desc: Every export tests the size of its filtered set against this before a file is generated. A change applies to exports requested after it.

interviews.title: Interviews
interviews.desc: The report clock and the rebooking window. A change applies to interviews held / credits issued after it; one already running does not move.

fields.hint: FN:() => `How long an agent has to file a report after an interview is held. The candidate's report-ready promise is this plus the fixed ${REVIEW_WINDOW_HRS}-hour review window — currently ${SETTINGS.reportDeadline + REVIEW_WINDOW_HRS} hours.`
How long a candidate has to use a rebooking credit or free rebooking after a failed or cancelled interview.

cohorts.title: Cohorts
cohorts.desc: Session-room rules. A session captures these at the moment it is held and keeps them; a change applies to sessions held after it and never rewrites a register already written.

fields.hint: Time in the room (counted cumulatively across the session) to count as having attended it.
How long a room stays open after the leader’s connection drops before it closes and the register is written.

tal.title: Tal
tal.desc: The Ask Tal ceiling — each question is a call the platform pays for. Counted per candidate per calendar day in their own time zone. A change applies to days beginning after it.

fields.hint: A suggestion chip counts against it. Tal’s compulsory onboarding conversation is outside this limit.

closure.title: Account closure and deactivation
closure.desc: How long an external account stays Deactivated after administrator deactivation or self-closure before it moves automatically to Deleted. A change applies to deactivations committed after it.

fields.hint: Reactivating during the grace period cancels the move to Deleted. An internal account stays Deactivated indefinitely.

TX_LINES_ADM: Before we start, nothing here is a test you can fail. Tell me about a handover you planned rather than announced.
The vendor review. I wrote down who owned each thread and set two checkpoints before I handed it over.
Who did it go to, and what did you keep hold of?
It went to my second, Sam. I kept the two checkpoints and the final sign-off, nothing in between.
Tell me about a conversation you had to open yourself, one nobody handed you.
Honestly, most of those came to me. I handle them once they land, but I could be earlier.
When a deadline moved on that review, who made the call to change scope?
I did. I cut the second checkpoint rather than push the date, and told the team why the same afternoon.
If I am honest, I planned the handover well but I did not start the hard conversation that the delay needed.
What would you do differently next time?
Name the problem before it is urgent, and ask for the time I need instead of absorbing it.
